period: Ptolemaic and early Roman, mostly 2nd-1st century BC
summary: A small late temple where the priests taught that dead Osiris entered the body of a hippo goddess and was reborn as Amun.
look: A compact sandstone temple pressed against the west side of the Temple of Khonsu, raised on a tall platform. The door is often locked; if a guard is about, ask politely. Inside, the reliefs are crisp, and crypts lie below the sanctuary.
story:
Opet, or Ipet, was a hippopotamus goddess, a protector of birth like her cousin Taweret. Late Theban priests gave her a cosmic job: she was the mother in whose body the dead Osiris was reborn, and in their theology Osiris and Amun became two phases of one god.

The temple was begun under Ptolemy VIII in the 2nd century BC and decorated by later Ptolemies, with work continuing into Roman times. It stands on a high podium, and the crypts under the floor were treated as the tomb of Osiris. So you climb up to the house of the mother and go down into the tomb of the god: death and birth in one building, which was exactly the point.

The late relief here is among the finest at Karnak, and almost nobody sees it.
details: The high podium: the floor sits well above the ground around it, a raised house for the divine mother.
If you get inside, ask about the crypts below the sanctuary, treated as the tomb of Osiris.
Compare the soft, rounded late figures here with the crisper New Kingdom reliefs in Khonsu's temple next door.
It stands right against the Khonsu temple: walk round Khonsu's west side to find it.
fun_fact: The priests mapped a whole life cycle onto one small building: Osiris goes into a hippo's womb as a dead king and comes out as Amun, ready to rule again.
narration: This small, tall temple pressed against the Temple of Khonsu belongs to Opet, a hippopotamus goddess of birth. Late Egyptian priests gave her a grand role. She was the mother in whose body the dead Osiris was reborn, and he came out as Amun, king of the gods. So the building is a womb and a tomb at once. It was begun under Ptolemy the Eighth, in the second century BC, and decorated by later kings. It stands on a high platform, and crypts under the floor were treated as the tomb of Osiris. The door is often locked, so ask a guard politely. Look at the raised platform: you climb up to the mother's house, and go down to the god's tomb.

period: New Kingdom, Thutmose III, c. 1450 BC, with Kushite and Ptolemaic gates
summary: A tiny temple at the northern edge of Karnak where a black granite lioness stands in a dark room, lit only by a shaft of light from the roof.
look: A small temple against the northern enclosure wall of the Amun precinct, entered through a line of six little gateways one behind the other. The sanctuary has three chapels: headless Ptah in the middle, Sekhmet in the right-hand one. Her room has no window, only an opening in the roof, so let your eyes adjust before you go in.
story:
Ptah was the creator god of Memphis, a craftsman who made the world by thinking it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue. His wife was Sekhmet, the lioness, and their son Nefertem, the lotus. Karnak belonged to Amun, but Thebes kept a house for the Memphite family too. A shrine stood here early; Thutmose III rebuilt it in stone, and the Kushite king Shabaka and several Ptolemies added the chain of gateways you walk through. Ptolemy III and IV did most of the late work on the court.

Sekhmet, 'the powerful one', was the Eye of Ra in his angry form. In one myth Ra sent her to punish rebellious humans and she would not stop killing, so the gods poured out a lake of beer dyed red with ochre. She drank it as if it were blood, got drunk and calmed down. She sent plague, and she was also the one people asked to cure it.

Her statue stands in black granite, lion-headed, a sun disc on her head. The light from the roof falls differently through the day, and the effect is uncanny. You may hear local stories that she was feared in the villages and once attacked; treat them as folklore, but you will understand them when you are alone with her.

A guard usually holds the key. Expect to tip him for opening up; it is part of the visit and worth it.
details: Count the gateways: six in a row, from a Ptolemaic one at the front to the inner ones. Shabaka's name is on two of them.
On the jambs of the first gate, the son Nefertem holds a blue lotus, the flower of the first sunrise.
Central chapel: the headless statue of Ptah. Right-hand chapel: Sekhmet in black granite with a sun disc on her head.
Look up in Sekhmet's room for the opening in the roof: the only light, so the effect changes through the day.
Skip the phone torch if you can: wait a minute in the dark and let the roof light do the work.
fun_fact: Sekhmet's priests were among Egypt's healers: the goddess who sent the plague was the one you paid to stop it.
narration: You are at the Temple of Ptah, a small house for a family from the north, tucked against the edge of Amun's city. Ptah was the creator god of Memphis, the craftsman who made the world by thinking it and speaking it. His wife was Sekhmet, the lioness, and their son was Nefertem, the lotus flower. A shrine stood here early. Thutmose the Third rebuilt it in stone about 1450 BC, and later kings, the Nubian pharaoh Shabaka and several Ptolemies, added the line of little gates you walk through, six of them one behind the other. Inside are three chapels. In the middle stands Ptah, without his head. On the right is the reason people come: Sekhmet in black granite, standing in a room with no window, lit only by an opening in the roof. Her name means the powerful one. In one myth the sun god sent her to punish rebellious humans, and she would not stop killing. So the gods poured out a lake of beer dyed red. She drank it, thinking it was blood, fell asleep drunk, and humanity survived. She sent plague, and she was also the goddess you begged to cure it. The guard keeps the key, so a small tip is part of the visit. Step into her room, wait for your eyes to adjust, and watch the light from the roof fall on her face.

period: Third Intermediate Period, 23rd to 25th Dynasties, 8th century BC
summary: A little chapel where the real powers in Thebes are two princesses, the God's Wives of Amun, performing rites that elsewhere only kings perform.
look: A small stone chapel with a mud-brick surround, in the quiet north-eastern part of the precinct, out beyond the Festival Hall of Thutmose III towards the enclosure wall. Coloured reliefs survive inside. It is often locked; if it is open, look for women in tall plumed crowns.
story:
Osiris Heqadjet means 'Osiris, Ruler of Eternity'. In the centuries after the New Kingdom, Osiris worship spread through Karnak, and small chapels to different forms of the god went up around the great temple. This one was built under the Libyan kings Osorkon III and Takelot III and enlarged under the Kushite kings who followed.

Its real interest is who appears on its walls. Osorkon III made his daughter Shepenupet I God's Wife of Amun: a royal princess, unmarried, who controlled the god's estate in Thebes and passed the office on by adoption. When the Kushite king Kashta extended his power to Thebes, he had Shepenupet adopt his own daughter, Amenirdis I, as her successor. Here both women perform rituals and offer to the gods with the authority that elsewhere belongs to kings and high priests.

It is a political document in stone: a Libyan princess and a Nubian princess sharing a wall, the handover of Thebes made polite.
details: Look for the God's Wives: women wearing a tall double-plumed crown, offering to the gods exactly as a pharaoh would.
Cartouches of the Libyan kings Osorkon III and Takelot III mark the original chapel.
Notice the mix of mud brick and stone: modest building for a modest age, with fine relief inside.
Other small Osiris chapels of the same era stand in ruins around the precinct; this is among the best preserved.
fun_fact: A God's Wife of Amun had to stay unmarried, so the job passed by adoption: any king who wanted Thebes made sure his daughter got adopted.
narration: This modest chapel belongs to Osiris Heqadjet, which means Osiris, Ruler of Eternity. It dates from the eighth century BC, when Egypt was split between rival kings. Osiris worship was growing, and small chapels to him sprang up around Karnak. This one was built under the Libyan kings Osorkon the Third and Takelot the Third, and enlarged under the Nubian kings who followed. Its walls show the God's Wives of Amun. A God's Wife was a royal princess, unmarried, who controlled the god's vast estate at Thebes and performed rituals usually done by kings. She chose her successor by adoption. Osorkon placed his daughter Shepenupet in the post. When the Nubian king Kashta reached Thebes, he had Shepenupet adopt his own daughter, Amenirdis. So a Libyan princess and a Nubian princess share these walls, the handover of a city made polite. The chapel is often locked. If you can see inside, look for women wearing a tall double feather crown, standing before the gods just as a pharaoh would.

period: Middle and New Kingdom chapels, about 1950 to 1390 BC
summary: Kings demolished their ancestors' chapels and stuffed them inside new pylons. Archaeologists pulled them out and rebuilt them here, block by block.
look: A walled garden in the north-west corner of the Amun precinct, to the left of the Great Court as you come in. Rebuilt chapels stand in the open: the White Chapel of Senusret I, the Red Chapel of Hatshepsut, the alabaster chapel of Amenhotep I and others, with rows of loose blocks on low benches all around. Allow 45 minutes.
story:
Egyptian kings rarely threw good stone away. When a ruler wanted a bigger gateway, he often dismantled the chapels of his predecessors and used the blocks as fill inside the new pylon's towers. For the builders it was cheap and quick, and perhaps even pious, since the sacred stones stayed inside the god's house. For archaeologists it was a gift: the fill protected the carving from weather and from later hammers. Amenhotep III's Third Pylon turned out to be a time capsule.

From the 1920s, French and Egyptian teams working at Karnak, Henri Chevrier among them, opened pylons and found whole buildings in pieces. The White Chapel of Senusret I came out of the Third Pylon in 1927. Blocks of Hatshepsut's Red Chapel turned up in several places, many in the 1950s, and a French-Egyptian team completed its reconstruction in 1997 with more than 300 blocks. The museum also holds the alabaster chapel of Amenhotep I, a calcite shrine of Amenhotep II, a barque shrine of Thutmose III and Thutmose IV's barque chapel, all rebuilt from salvaged pieces.

The blocks lined up on benches are the unfinished jigsaw: decorated stones still waiting to be matched. Some will never find their neighbours.

It is the quietest corner of Karnak, with grass, some shade and few crowds, and it puts Middle Kingdom and early 18th Dynasty carving at eye level.
details: The White Chapel: the small white kiosk on a platform with ramps, nearly 4,000 years old. Start here.
The Red Chapel: the long shrine of Hatshepsut in red quartzite above a black stone base.
The alabaster chapel of Amenhotep I: translucent white calcite from the very start of the New Kingdom.
The rows of blocks on benches: look for half-figures and cut-off hieroglyphs still missing their neighbours.
Check your ticket: this garden has usually needed its own ticket from the main Karnak office.
fun_fact: The best-preserved chapels at Karnak survived because later kings wrecked them: inside a pylon is the safest place for a relief to spend 3,000 years.
narration: Welcome to the Open Air Museum, the quiet garden in the north-west corner of Karnak where demolished buildings have come back to life. Egyptian kings rarely wasted good stone. When a pharaoh wanted a new gateway, he often took apart the chapels of earlier kings and packed the blocks inside his pylon as fill. That was bad news for the old chapels and wonderful news for us, because the fill protected the carving from sun, rain and later hammers for more than 3,000 years. Amenhotep the Third's Third Pylon turned out to be a time capsule. From the 1920s, French and Egyptian archaeologists working at Karnak opened the pylons and found whole buildings in pieces. The White Chapel of Senusret the First came out in 1927. The Red Chapel of Hatshepsut was rebuilt from more than 300 blocks and finished in 1997. Around them stand other rescued shrines: an alabaster chapel of Amenhotep the First, a calcite shrine of Amenhotep the Second, and boat shrines of Thutmose the Third and Thutmose the Fourth. The rows of stones on low benches are the unfinished puzzle, carved blocks still waiting for their neighbours. This garden has usually needed its own ticket, so check yours. Then start at the small white kiosk on its platform with ramps: the White Chapel, nearly 4,000 years old.

period: Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, Senusret I, c. 1950 BC
summary: Karnak's oldest standing building: a jubilee kiosk of about 1950 BC, taken apart, buried in a pylon, and rebuilt with carving as sharp as the day it was cut.
look: A small, square limestone kiosk on a raised platform, with a ramp at each end and square pillars carved on every face. Walk round the pillars: on each side the king meets a god. Along the outside of the base runs a band of emblems and text listing the provinces of Egypt.
story:
Senusret I, second king of the 12th Dynasty, built this kiosk for his jubilee, the Sed festival that renewed a king's power after years on the throne. It probably served as a resting station where Amun's barque could pause during processions. It is fine white limestone, hence the name.

About 550 years later, Amenhotep III needed fill for his new Third Pylon and had the chapel dismantled. Its blocks lay inside the pylon until 1927, when they were found during Henri Chevrier's work at Karnak, and over the following years they were taken out and the chapel rebuilt here, almost complete. Today it is the oldest building standing at Karnak; the Middle Kingdom temple it served has vanished down to its foundations.

The relief is the finest Middle Kingdom work you will see on this trip. On the pillars Senusret is crowned and embraced by Amun, Horus, Min and Ptah. Min, the fertility god, stands with his erect phallus and one arm raised behind him holding a flail. Around the base, the provinces of Upper Egypt run along the west side and those of Lower Egypt along the east, each with its emblem and god: a geography lesson carved four thousand years ago.
details: On the pillar faces, find Amun embracing the king, and Min with his raised arm, flail and erect phallus.
Base of the outer walls: the list of provinces, each with its emblem. Upper Egypt on the west side, Lower Egypt on the east.
Get close to one hieroglyph, an owl or a quail chick: feathers and eyes carved with jeweller's precision.
Limestone takes finer detail than Karnak's usual sandstone: compare it with the columns of the Hypostyle Hall.
fun_fact: Min's sacred plant was lettuce: the tall Egyptian kind oozes a milky sap, and the Egyptians considered it an aphrodisiac.
narration: This small white kiosk on its platform is the oldest building still standing at Karnak. It was built about 1950 BC by Senusret the First, a king of the Middle Kingdom, for his jubilee, the festival that renewed a king's power after many years of rule. Amun's sacred boat probably rested here during processions. It is made of fine limestone, hence the name, the White Chapel. About 550 years later, Amenhotep the Third needed fill for a new pylon and had it taken apart. Its blocks lay hidden inside the Third Pylon until 1927, when the French team led by Henri Chevrier found them, and it was rebuilt here almost complete. That burial saved it. The carving is as sharp as any you will see in Egypt. Walk round the pillars. On each face Senusret meets a god. Amun embraces him, Horus and Ptah greet him, and Min, the fertility god, stands with his erect phallus and one arm raised. Around the base runs a list of the provinces of Egypt, each with its emblem and its god, Upper Egypt on one side and Lower Egypt on the other. It is a map of the country in stone, 4,000 years old. Now look closely at a single hieroglyph, an owl or a quail chick, and see the feathers carved in limestone.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Hatshepsut, c. 1460 BC
summary: Hatshepsut's shrine for Amun's boat, torn down after her death and rebuilt from 300 blocks: a strip cartoon of her festivals and her claim to be king.
look: A long, low shrine of dark red quartzite on a black stone base, about 18 m long, 6 m wide and 5.5 m high. The reliefs run in horizontal bands like a comic strip, and the best scenes are on the outside walls. Walk slowly along both long sides.
story:
Hatshepsut began this shrine in her 17th regnal year to house the barque of Amun, the gilded boat in which the god's statue travelled. It stood in the heart of Karnak, in front of the old Middle Kingdom temple. The walls were red quartzite, the base black diorite and granite, a costly combination.

The reliefs are her propaganda. Priests carry the barque through Thebes in the Opet Festival and the Beautiful Festival of the Valley. She runs her jubilee race beside the Apis bull. Her obelisks are brought from Aswan. Other blocks describe how Amun chose her as king, and her daughter Neferure appears as God's Wife of Amun. Hatshepsut is usually shown in the dress and regalia of a male king. Her stepson Thutmose III appears too, and his name was added on the upper blocks.

After her death Thutmose III dismantled the chapel, perhaps to make room for a granite shrine of his own. Her names were later hacked out, patchily, apparently after the blocks were already down. The pieces were reused: two black granite doorways in his own buildings, many blocks inside Amenhotep III's Third Pylon, others in later foundations. Many were rediscovered in the 1950s, and in 1997 a French-Egyptian team completed the reconstruction you see, displaying more than 300 blocks.

Come here on the same day as Luxor Temple: the processions carved in its colonnade are drawn here first.
details: Find Hatshepsut in a king's kilt and crown: only the hacked-out cartouches beside her give her away.
Look for Amun's barque carried on poles by rows of priests, with the veiled cabin in the middle.
Look for a figure striding beside a bull between field markers: the jubilee run with the Apis bull.
The black base: kneeling Nile gods and knotted plants run along the bottom of the walls.
Erasures: the chisel marks over her names are patchy, and many blocks are untouched on some faces.
fun_fact: The erasures give the game away: her names are hacked out on some faces of a block and untouched on others, which suggests the damage was done after the chapel was already in pieces.
narration: In front of you is the Red Chapel of Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled Egypt as king about 3,500 years ago. She began it in her seventeenth year as a shrine for Amun's sacred boat, the gilded barque in which the god's statue travelled. It stood in the very heart of Karnak: red quartzite walls on a black stone base. The walls are a strip cartoon of her reign. Walk along the outside and you will see priests carrying the barque on poles during the Opet Festival and the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Hatshepsut running her jubilee race beside the Apis bull, and her obelisks brought from Aswan. Other scenes tell how Amun chose her as king. She is shown in a king's kilt and crown. Her stepson and co-ruler, Thutmose the Third, appears too. After her death he took the chapel down, perhaps to build a granite shrine of his own, and later her names were chiselled out, patchily, apparently after the blocks were already on the ground. The blocks were scattered as building fill, many inside Amenhotep the Third's Third Pylon. They were found over the years, especially in the 1950s, and a French and Egyptian team finished rebuilding the chapel in 1997. Now find a cartouche with a neat hole hacked into it, and the king beside it in a kilt: that is Hatshepsut.

period: Excavated 1903-1907; objects from the Old Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period
summary: Under this court Georges Legrain pulled nearly 800 stone statues and about 17,000 bronzes out of groundwater: the largest statue hoard ever found in Egypt.
look: The open court in front of the Seventh Pylon, on Karnak's north-south axis, just south of the Hypostyle Hall. Today it looks like any empty court; the pit lay in its north-western part. Ahead, the pylons of the south axis march towards the Precinct of Mut.
story:
In 1903 Georges Legrain, the Frenchman in charge of restoring Karnak, was clearing this court when statues began to appear in a pit. They kept coming until 1907. The pit lay below the water table, so the work went on in mud and groundwater, the men feeling for stone before hauling each piece out. The final count was nearly 800 stone statues, more than 350 of them block statues, and about 17,000 bronzes and other objects, ranging from the Old Kingdom to the end of the Ptolemaic period.

Why were they there? Over the centuries, officials and priests crowded the temple with statues of themselves, and sacred objects could not simply be thrown away. It is generally believed that priests buried the surplus here in one ritual clear-out in the Ptolemaic period.

Most pieces went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, others to museums around the world, and the Luxor Museum's Thutmose III comes from here. Legrain's excavation diaries and master list are lost, but more than 1,200 photographs survive, and scholars are still matching statues to them. Legrain died in Luxor in 1917.
details: Picture the pit in the north-west part of the court: statues came out of it for four seasons, 1903 to 1907.
On the court's walls, Merneptah recorded his victories, including over the Sea Peoples.
Look south through the Seventh Pylon: this processional axis leads towards the temple of Mut, Amun's wife.
Block statues, over 350 of the finds, show a man squatting as a cube, only head, hands and feet showing.
fun_fact: Legrain's diaries and his master list of the hoard are lost, so a century later Egyptologists still identify statues by matching them to his old photographs.
narration: You are standing in the Cachette Court, in front of the Seventh Pylon on Karnak's north-south axis. It looks empty. In 1903 it was the scene of the biggest statue find ever made in Egypt. Georges Legrain, the French archaeologist in charge of restoring Karnak, was clearing the court when statues began to appear in a pit. They kept coming until 1907. The pit lay below the water table, so his workmen dug in mud and water, feeling for stone before hauling each piece out. The final count was nearly 800 stone statues and about 17,000 bronzes. Why bury them? Over the centuries, priests and officials crowded the temple with statues of themselves, and sacred objects could not just be thrown away. Most scholars think the priests buried the surplus here in one clear-out, in the Ptolemaic period. Most of the finds went to Cairo. Legrain's diaries are lost, but more than 1,200 of his photographs survive. Now look south through the Seventh Pylon: the processional way continues towards the temple of Mut, Amun's wife.

period: New Kingdom to Roman; Sekhmet statues of Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: Amun's wife had her own walled precinct, with a crescent-shaped sacred lake and hundreds of black lion-headed goddesses sitting in the grass.
look: A separate walled enclosure about 325 m south of the Amun precinct, covering about 9 hectares. The Temple of Mut sits in the middle, wrapped on three sides by its crescent lake, Isheru. Black granite Sekhmet statues sit and stand around the courts, many broken, some intact. Access has changed over the years: ask at the Karnak ticket office.
story:
Mut, 'mother', was Amun's wife and the mother of Khonsu; together they formed the Theban triad. She could appear as a vulture or a lioness, and as Thebes grew she absorbed the fierce goddess Sekhmet. Many kings built here: the earliest cartouches are of the Thutmosids, Hatshepsut added what an inscription calls a 'porch of drunkenness', Ramesses II and Ramesses III built temples in the precinct, and the Kushite king Taharqa added a new gateway.

Amenhotep III commissioned hundreds of granite statues of Sekhmet, the lioness who brought plague. One popular theory says there were about 730, one for each day and each night of the year, each receiving a prayer to keep her calm. Some may have been brought from his mortuary temple across the river. Museums worldwide own dozens; the British Museum alone has about thirty.

The first excavators, in 1895-97, were two Englishwomen, Margaret Benson and Janet Gourlay. The Brooklyn Museum worked here from 1976, and Johns Hopkins University under Betsy Bryan from 2001. Bryan's team found evidence of a festival of drunkenness, when crowds drank to soothe the lioness, echoing the myth in which red beer saved humanity from her rage.
details: The crescent lake, Isheru, curving round the temple on three sides: the goddess's own sacred water.
Sekhmet statues: lion head, woman's body, sun disc on the head. Count how many you can find still sitting in place.
West of the lake, the ruined temple of Ramesses III, with two headless colossi of the king at its door.
Taharqa's gateway in the north-west, built when the Kushite king enlarged the precinct.
fun_fact: Margaret Benson, who led the first dig here in the 1890s, was a sister of E. F. Benson, the author of the Mapp and Lucia novels.
narration: This is the Precinct of Mut, the walled home of Amun's wife, a few hundred metres south of the great temple. Mut means mother. With Amun and their son Khonsu she made up the divine family of Thebes, and she had a fierce side: she absorbed Sekhmet, the lioness goddess of plague. That is why the courts are full of black granite statues with a lion's head and a woman's body. Amenhotep the Third had hundreds of them carved. One popular theory says there were about 730, one for each day and each night of the year, each with a prayer to calm her. Dozens more now sit in museums around the world. The temple is wrapped on three sides by a crescent-shaped sacred lake. The first people to dig here, in 1895, were two Englishwomen, Margaret Benson and Janet Gourlay. A century later a team from Johns Hopkins found traces of a festival of drunkenness, when crowds drank to soothe the lioness, just as beer had once saved humanity from her rage. Find one Sekhmet still sitting in the grass, and look at the sun disc on her head.

period: New Kingdom (Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC) with a Ptolemaic gate
summary: The old war god of Thebes kept his own temple north of Amun's, and a small temple here once hosted the trials of tomb robbers.
look: A walled enclosure of about 2 hectares against the north side of the Amun precinct. It is usually closed, but from inside Karnak you can see its tall Ptolemaic gateway, Bab el-Abd, rising over the wall. Behind it lie the low ruins of Amenhotep III's temple.
story:
Montu, the falcon-headed god of war, was lord of Thebes before Amun rose to the top. The 11th Dynasty kings who reunited Egypt around 2000 BC carried his name: Mentuhotep means 'Montu is content'.

Amenhotep III rebuilt a Middle Kingdom sanctuary here for Montu-Ra, Ramesses II added a forecourt and two obelisks, and Ptolemy III and IV built the great gate, reached by an avenue from a quay. Nearby stood a small temple of Maat, goddess of truth and order, where under Ramesses IX a court tried the robbers of royal tombs. Most of the precinct is poorly preserved and closed to visitors.
details: From the northern side of the Amun precinct, look for the tall stone gateway above the wall: Ptolemy III and IV's gate.
Montu in reliefs: a falcon head crowned with a sun disc and two tall plumes.
Mentuhotep, 'Montu is content': Mentuhotep II's temple is the one you saw beside Hatshepsut's at Deir el-Bahari.
fun_fact: The famous tomb-robbery trials of about 1110 BC were heard in a little temple of Maat, the goddess of truth, inside this precinct.
narration: Beyond the north wall of Amun's precinct lies the Precinct of Montu, the falcon-headed war god who was lord of Thebes before Amun took over. The kings who reunited Egypt around 2000 BC were named after him: Mentuhotep means Montu is content. Amenhotep the Third rebuilt his temple here, Ramesses the Second added obelisks, and Ptolemy the Third and Fourth built the tall gateway that rises above the wall. In a small temple of Maat, goddess of truth, judges once tried the men who robbed royal tombs. The precinct is usually closed. Look north over the enclosure wall for the top of that Ptolemaic gate.

summary: A small museum that chose quality over quantity: a few hundred masterpieces, lit like jewels, and an air-conditioned break from the midday sun.
look: A low modern building on the Corniche, between Luxor Temple and Karnak, facing the Nile. Inside: a dark, calm ground floor of big statues, an upper floor, the hall of the 1989 Luxor Temple statues, and a newer wing on the early New Kingdom army with two royal mummies. Plan 1 to 1.5 hours.
story:
The Ministry of Culture commissioned the architect Mahmoud El-Hakim in 1962; the objects were installed between 1972 and 1975, and the museum opened in 1975. The idea was the opposite of the crowded old Cairo museum: fewer pieces, each with space, good light and clear labels. It works. You can see everything that matters without museum fatigue.

Two additions changed it. In 1989 workers at Luxor Temple found a pit of buried statues, and a hall was built for them here. In March 2004 a new wing opened on the military glory of the early New Kingdom, with chariots and weapons, and two royal mummies: Ahmose I, who drove out the Hyksos, and the mummy believed to be Ramesses I, back from more than a century at Niagara Falls.

A good route: the calcite Sobek with Amenhotep III; the tall limestone stela of Kamose from Karnak, telling of the war against the Hyksos; Thutmose III in greywacke; the Akhenaten wall; the scribe statue of Amenhotep son of Hapu; any Tutankhamun pieces still here; the cachette hall; and the mummies in the new wing. Come in the midday heat, between Karnak in the morning and Luxor Temple at dusk.
details: The calcite Sobek and Amenhotep III: the crocodile god and the king side by side, a good place to start.
The Kamose stela: 2.3 m of limestone from Karnak, the war on the Hyksos told for the king just before Ahmose.
The Akhenaten wall: hundreds of small blocks from his Karnak temple, reassembled into one long painted wall.
The cachette hall: the 1989 statues from under Luxor Temple, with Amenhotep III on his sledge.
The military wing: chariots, weapons and two royal mummies in a dim room.
fun_fact: One of the kings in the new wing spent more than 130 years in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls before researchers worked out who he probably was.
narration: Welcome to the Luxor Museum, opened in 1975 and designed around a simple idea: show fewer things, and show them beautifully. Dark walls, careful spotlights, plenty of space. You can see everything that matters in an hour or so, and it is the best place in Luxor to spend the hottest part of the day. Here is a route. Near the start, the white calcite statue of the crocodile god Sobek with King Amenhotep the Third. Look for the tall stela of Kamose, the king who fought the Hyksos invaders just before Ahmose finished the job. Then Thutmose the Third, the conqueror, in dark polished stone, and the long wall of small painted blocks from Akhenaten's lost temple at Karnak. Find the scribe statue of Amenhotep son of Hapu, the architect who became a god. In 1989 workers at Luxor Temple found a pit full of buried statues, and a special hall was built here for them; its star is Amenhotep the Third in red quartzite, standing on a sledge. Finally, in the newer wing opened in 2004, chariots, weapons and two royal mummies: Ahmose the First, and the man believed to be Ramesses the First, who spent more than a century in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls. Start with Sobek: look for the crocodile head, and the small king at his side.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC; later inscribed by Ramesses II
summary: A crocodile-headed god and a young king carved from one block of glowing calcite, found by chance in 1967 at the bottom of a water-filled shaft.
look: A group carved from a single block of calcite, the stone called Egyptian alabaster. Sobek, with a man's body and a crocodile's head under a tall crown, sits on a throne, with Amenhotep III beside him at a much smaller scale. Step to one side where the light passes into the stone's thin edges: it glows.
story:
Sobek was the crocodile god, lord of the waters and of the fertility the Nile brought, and crocodiles were a real danger on every riverbank. At Sumenu, south of Thebes near Armant, he had an important cult centre, and this statue comes from there. The king is beside the seated god at a much smaller scale, like a protected son: the power belongs to Sobek, and the king receives it.

It was found by chance in 1967 at Dahamsha, the site of ancient Sumenu, at the bottom of a shaft full of water, where it had lain since antiquity. Ramesses II later carved his own name on it, as he did on so many of his predecessors' statues: taking over a masterpiece was cheaper than commissioning one, and just as glorious.

Calcite is soft enough to carve fine detail and translucent enough to glow when light gets into it. Look at the king's face, round-cheeked with the almond eyes favoured by Amenhotep III's sculptors, and at the fine pleating of his kilt. Few statues put a god and a king so close together, and fewer still survive in this condition.
details: Sobek's head: a crocodile's long snout under a tall crown, on a muscular man's body.
Amenhotep III's face: round cheeks and almond eyes, the house style of his reign.
Stand where a light is behind a thin edge of stone: calcite is translucent and seems to glow from inside.
Search the inscriptions for Ramesses II's cartouches, added long after Amenhotep III's death.
Compare with the crocodile mummies you saw at Kom Ombo's Crocodile Museum on the 20th.
fun_fact: Herodotus, visiting Egypt in the 5th century BC, describes tame sacred crocodiles wearing earrings of glass and gold, with bracelets on their front feet.
narration: Here is one of the finest statues of the New Kingdom: the crocodile god Sobek, seated on a throne, with King Amenhotep the Third beside him, both carved from a single block of calcite, the stone often called Egyptian alabaster. Sobek has a man's body and a crocodile's head under a tall crown. The king is smaller and young-faced, close to the god like a protected son. The message is clear: the power comes from the god, and the king receives it. Sobek ruled the Nile's waters and the crocodiles that lived in them, a very real danger on every riverbank. One of his cult centres was Sumenu, south of Thebes, and that is where this statue comes from. It was found by chance in 1967 at Dahamsha, the site of Sumenu, at the bottom of a shaft full of water, where it had lain since antiquity. Later, Ramesses the Second added his own name to it, as he did to so many of his predecessors' statues. The Greek historian Herodotus, visiting Egypt in the fifth century BC, saw tame sacred crocodiles wearing earrings of glass and gold, with bracelets on their front feet. Now look at the king's face, round-cheeked with almond eyes, then step to the side, where the light passes into the thin stone and makes it glow.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose III, 1479-1425 BC
summary: The face of Egypt's greatest conqueror, carved in dark greywacke with a gentle half-smile you would never expect from a man who spent twenty years at war.
look: A statue of Thutmose III in dark, fine-grained greywacke, polished to a soft sheen, from the Karnak cachette. He wears the striped nemes headcloth with the cobra on his brow and a pleated kilt. Look at the face first, then search the belt and inscriptions for his name in a cartouche.
story:
Thutmose III came to the throne as a child in 1479 BC, and for about 22 years his stepmother and aunt Hatshepsut ruled beside him, in the end as senior king. When she died around 1458 BC he went to war almost at once. In his year 23 he led his army through a narrow mountain pass his generals thought too dangerous, routed a coalition of Canaanite princes at Megiddo, and then besieged the city for seven or eight months. Over the next twenty years he campaigned again and again, at least sixteen times by most counts, and in year 33 he carried boats overland to cross the Euphrates and strike at Mitanni. The American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt. His annals are carved on the walls of the Amun temple at Karnak.

None of that shows in this face. The sculptors of his family gave their kings a calm, youthful look: almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and a faint smile. It is an ideal, not a photograph, but the family likeness runs through the dynasty.

The statue was found in the Karnak cachette, the great hoard of buried statues that Georges Legrain recovered from 1903. Greywacke, a hard dark stone from the Wadi Hammamat in the Eastern Desert, takes a polish that catches the light.

His throne name, Menkheperre, roughly 'the manifestation of Ra is established', became the favourite royal name on scarab amulets, copied for centuries after his death.
details: The face: almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and the closed half-smile of the Thutmoside kings.
The nemes headcloth with its stripes, and the cobra rising on his brow.
Menkheperre in a cartouche: a sun disc, a scarab beetle and a sign like a game board. Look for it on the statue.
The polish: hard greywacke from the Eastern Desert takes a sheen that sandstone never could.
fun_fact: Menkheperre was such a lucky name that Egyptians kept putting it on scarab amulets for centuries after his death, and you will still see it on souvenir scarabs today.
narration: Meet Thutmose the Third, carved in dark greywacke and polished until it shines. He came to the throne as a small child in 1479 BC. For about twenty years his stepmother and aunt, Hatshepsut, ruled beside him, and in the end above him. When she died, he went to war. In his twenty-third year he led his army through a narrow mountain pass that his generals called too dangerous, surprised an alliance of Canaanite princes at Megiddo, and then besieged the city for seven months or more. Over the next twenty years he campaigned again and again, at least sixteen times, and once he carried boats overland so his army could cross the Euphrates. The American Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt. Yet look at this face. Calm, young, with almond eyes, a slightly hooked nose and a faint smile. The sculptors of his family gave every king this serene look; it is an ideal, not a photograph. The statue comes from the Karnak cachette, the pit of buried statues found by Georges Legrain in 1903. Now look for his throne name, Menkheperre, written in a cartouche with a sun disc, a scarab beetle and a sign shaped like a game board. It became the favourite name on lucky scarab amulets for centuries, and you will still see it on souvenir scarabs today.
